card.title: Electric Field due to Point Charges

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: The electric field E is a vector field describing electrostatic force per unit test charge (E = F/q₀). Point charges produce radially symmetric fields falling off as 1/r², mapped visually by continuous non-intersecting field lines originating on positive and terminating on negative charges.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Electric field definition: $\vec{E} = \frac{\vec{F}}{q_0}$
Field of a point charge: $\vec{E} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2}\hat{r}$
Electric dipole moment: $\vec{p} = q(2\vec{a})$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: Confusing field line direction with trajectory of a moving charge: An electric field line represents the direction of electrostatic force on a stationary positive charge, NOT the trajectory of a moving charge. A moving charge accelerates along $\vec{F} = q\vec{E}$, so velocity and field vectors generally diverge due to inertia.  ·  Assuming field lines can intersect: If two field lines crossed, a test charge at the intersection would experience two distinct electrostatic forces in different directions simultaneously, which violates the uniqueness theorem of vector fields.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Electrostatic field lines do not form closed loops because electrostatic fields are conservative: the closed loop line integral ∮ E · dr = 0.  ·  A charged particle projected perpendicularly into a uniform electric field follows a parabolic trajectory, analogous to projectile motion in a uniform gravitational field.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Inkjet printers: Electrically deflected microscopic ink droplets pass between high-voltage deflection plates generating a uniform electric field, steering droplets precisely onto paper to render text and images.  ·  Cathode Ray Oscilloscope (CRO): An electron beam accelerated by an electron gun is deflected horizontally and vertically by orthogonal electric fields between parallel plates, projecting waveforms onto a fluorescent screen.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Confusing the radial fall-off of dipoles versus point charges: Point charge field scales as $1/r^2$, whereas an electric dipole field decays as $1/r^3$ because the positive and negative charges largely cancel each other out at long distances ($r \gg a$).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Derive expressions for E_axial and E_equatorial of an electric dipole.  ·  Sketch electric field lines for unlike charges, like charges, and uniform fields.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Dipole field ratio trick: At identical large distance r, E_axial / E_equatorial = 2.  ·  Neutral point between like charges: E_net = 0 lies between them at distance x = d / (√(q₂/q₁) + 1) from q₁.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Q1. Define electric field intensity. Derive an expression for the electric field at a distance r due to an isolated point charge Q in vacuum.  ·  Q2. State four essential characteristics of electric field lines and explain why two field lines can never intersect each other.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Derivation of electric field due to an electric dipole at axial and equatorial points is a premier 4-mark question in NEB Class 11 Physics exams.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Definition and physical meaning of electric field vector E = F/q₀.  ·  Electric field of a point charge and principle of linear superposition.  ·  Rules governing electric field lines and why they never form closed loops.  ·  Electric dipole moment and derivation of axial and equatorial dipole fields.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Electric field intensity is force per unit positive test charge ($E = F/q_0$) in N/C or V/m.  ·  Point charge field obeys inverse square law ($E \propto 1/r^2$); short dipole field obeys inverse cube law ($E \propto 1/r^3$).  ·  Field lines point outward from positive charges and inward toward negative charges, never intersecting.  ·  Axial field of a short dipole is exactly twice the magnitude of equatorial field at equal distance ($E_{axial} = 2 E_{equatorial}$).

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The terrestrial fair-weather atmosphere maintains a downward-directed vertical electric field of approximately $100\,\text{to}\,150\,\text{V/m}$ near the Earth's surface due to the global electrical thunderstorm battery circuit.  ·  Electric fields in nerve cells (action potentials) reach immense intensities of roughly $10^7\,\text{V/m}$ across thin ($7\text{ nm}$) phospholipid bilayer cell membranes, driving ion pumps that enable animal thought and heartbeat.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Q3. Define electric dipole moment. Derive expressions for the electric field intensity due to a short electric dipole at (a) an axial point, and (b) an equatorial point.  ·  Q4. An electron is released from rest in a uniform horizontal electric field of intensity 2.0 × 10⁴ N/C. Calculate its acceleration and the time taken to travel a distance of 1.5 cm.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Laser toner transfer: Controlled electrostatic fields attract charged polymer toner particles from the photoconductor drum onto paper, which is subsequently thermally fused.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: The electric field intensity at an axial point distance r from a short electric dipole is E. The electric field at an equatorial point at the same distance r is: → B  ·  An electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field experiences: → C

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Electric Field Concept & Definition:** An electric field $\vec{E}$ is an intrinsic vector property of space surrounding any charged distribution. It is defined quantitatively as the electrostatic force experienced per unit positive infinitesimal test charge placed at that location: $\vec{E} = \lim_{q_0 \to 0} \frac{\vec{F}}{q_0}$.…  ·  **Electric Field due to an Isolated Point Charge:** Applying Coulomb's law to a source charge $q$ at position vector $\vec{r}'$ and test charge $q_0$ at field point $\vec{r}$, the electric field is: $\vec{E}(\vec{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{|\vec{r} - \vec{r}'|^3} (\vec{r} - \vec{r}') = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{q}{r^2}\hat{r}$.…  ·  **Superposition Principle for Discrete & Continuous Charges:** The net electric field created by an ensemble of $N$ discrete point charges is the vector sum of individual fields: $\vec{E}_{net} = \sum_{i=1}^N \vec{E}_i = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{q_i}{r_i^2}\hat{r}_i$.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Behavior of dipoles in uniform and non-uniform electric fields.  ·  Dipole field (axial, $r \gg a$): $\vec{E}_{axial} = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{2\vec{p}}{r^3}$  ·  Dipole field (equatorial, $r \gg a$): $\vec{E}_{equatorial} = -\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \frac{\vec{p}}{r^3}$

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Dipole torque in uniform field: $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$  ·  Dipole potential energy: $U = -\vec{p} \cdot \vec{E}$  ·  In a uniform electric field, an electric dipole experiences zero net force but a restoring torque $\vec{\tau} = \vec{p} \times \vec{E}$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Remember that the SI units N/C and V/m are completely interchangeable: 1 N/C = 1 (J/m) / C = 1 (J/C) / m = 1 V/m.  ·  Statement 1: The electric field at any point in space is the electrostatic force experienced per unit infinitesimal positive test charge.  ·  Statement 2: Electric field lines originate on positive charges, terminate on negative charges, and cannot intersect at any point.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 3: The electric field due to a point charge obeys an inverse-square distance relationship (E ∝ 1/r²).  ·  Statement 4: The electric field due to a short electric dipole decays inversely with the cube of distance (E ∝ 1/r³).  ·  Statement 5: In a uniform electric field, an electric dipole experiences zero translational net force but a net aligning torque τ = p × E.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Acceleration of charged particle in field: a = qE / m (direction along E for positive charge, opposite E for electron).  ·  Two point charges $q_1 = +5.0\,\mu\text{C}$ and $q_2 = -5.0\,\mu\text{C}$ are separated by $10\text{ cm}$ along the x-axis ($2a = 0.1\text{ m}$). (a) Find the electric dipole moment. (b) Find the electric field magnitude at an axial point $20\text{ cm}$ from the dipole center.…  ·  Calculate the net electric field and neutral point for two collinear point charges.
